# Second Saturday

Once a month, on a Saturday morning, our grounds and our practice are open to the wider community. Current families, former families, families who are curious about us, educators from other programs and local growers and makers share the same morning with children, materials and the season. It is our everyday practice with the gate open.

## What it holds to

- One shared experience mid-morning, arising from what the garden, farm and studio offer that season. Around it, an open environment of water, mud, loose parts, animals, building and art.
- Nobody has to take part in anything. A child who never joins the shared experience has missed nothing.
- The garden and the season decide. The month's inquiry is a starting point, and what the garden offers that day comes first.
- Materials are open-ended, with no single finished product.
- Visiting educators share the same space as families, with a short observation lens for the month.
- Our documentation is displayed in the environment so visitors meet our thinking.
- December, March, June and September are also the seasons' garden days.

## Before

- Two weeks before. Walk the garden with the garden lead, confirm the four roles, send the family announcement and check the supply list.
- The week of. Send a reminder, do the final garden walk, check the weather and plan shade or cover, and prepare the welcome, parking and wayfinding signs.
- The day before. Send the day-before reminder, set out baskets and boards, and check the sign-up list for allergies.

## Set up

- Open the grounds and put out the arrival signs.
- Set the stations for mud, water, loose parts, animals and art, as on any school day.
- Set the shared experience station for the month.
- Set the welcome table and display documentation from past mornings.
- Walk the whole site together for hazards, then confirm what is ripe, any allergy notes and each role.

## Who does what

- Shared experience lead. Holds the mid-morning gathering loosely and stands at the point of use for tools.
- Environment float. Moves through the stations and watches for safety across the grounds. It can be two people.
- Welcome. Check-in, greeting and questions about the morning.
- Community and educator host. Available to curious families, visiting educators and partners, while keeping an eye on the children.
- Roles rotate across our team so no one works every month.

## How the morning flows

- Arrival. No welcome speech. Families are greeted as they come in and move freely.
- Open environment. Educators quietly invite interest toward the shared experience as it begins.
- Shared experience. People come and go, and it stays open through the morning for families who arrive later.
- Close. A soft close. Stations wind down as the cue, and families are thanked as they leave.

## Our presence

- We are hosts and fellow researchers.
- We follow the child's interest, ask open questions and take children's theories seriously.
- We describe what we see, such as "She's testing how much water the sand can hold."
- We never stage photos or turn the morning into enrollment talk. Questions about enrolling go to the office.
- Conversations with visiting educators stay short and point to the observation lens and documentation.

## Supplies

- Kept all year. Harvest baskets, child-sized knives, peelers and graters, cutting boards, wash basins, bowls, long tables and covers, tarps, water tubs and channels, the loose parts crate, woodworking tools with goggles, pruners and twine, seed trays, magnifiers, pressing materials, shade canopies, a first aid kit for the day and reusable signs.
- Each month. Compostable plates and napkins, the month's food, seasonal natural materials, art and sensory supplies and printed observation cards.

## Safety

- Walk the site for hazards before opening.
- An adult at the point of use for every real tool.
- An educator near the animal areas when it is busy.
- Allergies collected at sign-up for any month with food. We are a nut free campus.
- A first aid trained educator on site the whole morning, and a headcount method for a drop-in crowd.
- Shade and water from June through September. Rain moves the shared experience under cover, and mud and water stations continue.
- Photos favor hands and materials. Children who are not enrolled are never shown by face in anything shared publicly.

## Cleanup

- Compost scraps, then wash and return tools.
- Collect linens, return loose parts and materials to storage and gather lost items.

## Afterward

A short team debrief, written into the gathering's Afterward in Gatherings.

- What happened that we did not plan for?
- What held children's attention longest, and why?
- Which conversations are worth following up?
- What would we change in setup, staffing or materials?
- Did anything feel over-directed?
- Any safety, weather or logistics notes for next month?
- One sentence for the archive.

# Play Garden

A morning outdoors in our garden and yards, open to every family from our school and beyond. A parent or caregiver stays with each child the whole time, and together we play, explore and care for the garden and the animals. Families apply through the Play Garden application, which the director turns on in Settings.

## What it holds to

- The whole morning is outdoors, rain or shine. The gazebo and the outdoor studio shed are our covered places in rain or strong sun.
- Children lead their own play, with open-ended materials and the living garden.
- Families take part in the life of the yard beside us.
- Our garden family agreements guide everyone. Pick with purpose and leave some for others. Be kind to all beings, the plants, the animals and nature.

## Before

- Check the applications and welcome each family.
- Send each family the date, what to wear, what to bring and our garden family agreements.
- Note any allergies or health needs from the applications for the educators on the day.
- Plan the morning's invitations from what the garden and season offer.

## Set up

- Walk the yard for hazards, such as holes, tools left out, wet areas, poison oak and poison hemlock.
- Set out loose parts, sand and digging tools, art materials in the studio shed and the snack station in the gazebo.
- Open the garden and animal areas only with an educator present.
- Set the welcome spot with a sign-in list.

## Who does what

- Lead educator. Welcomes families, holds the rhythm of the morning and is the point person for any concern.
- Garden educator. Stays with the garden beds and the animals.
- Studio and snack educator. The studio shed, the art materials and the snack.

## How the morning flows

- Welcome and sign-in.
- Open play across the yard, garden and studio.
- A gathering for snack in the gazebo, made from what is in season.
- More open play and garden care.
- Cleanup together and goodbye.

## Supplies

- Loose parts, sand tools, buckets and digging tools.
- Watering cans, garden gloves and baskets.
- Art materials for the studio shed.
- Snack, cups and napkins, and handwashing water.
- Sign-in list, first aid kit and sunscreen with permission.

## Safety

- Each parent or caregiver stays with their own child and takes them to the bathroom.
- Garden and animal areas open only with an educator present, and the chicken gate stays closed.
- An educator within arm's reach at the tire swing and at any climbing or risky play.
- A first aid and CPR trained educator on site the whole morning.
- We are a nut free campus, and snack follows the allergies families shared.
- Shoes in the garden and the animal yards.
- Photos for our own documentation only, unless a family agrees in writing.

## Cleanup

- Children and adults put materials away together.
- Empty and rinse the snack station, check the yard for anything left behind and close the gates.

## Afterward

Write what happened in the gathering's Afterward, with any incident, weather change or follow-up for the director.

# Garden visits

A class or group from another school comes to explore our garden. Their educator fills in the intake form before the first visit, and the form stays on paper with the visiting school. A garden visit stays with our staff.

## What it holds to

- Children explore the garden with their hands and senses.
- In educational gardening there is no failure. Everything is something to wonder about.
- Our garden agreements guide every visitor. Pick with purpose and leave some for others. Be kind to all beings, the plants, the animals and nature.

## Before

- Send the intake form to the visiting educator and confirm the day, group size, ages and allergies.
- Confirm the visiting school brings enough adults for one adult to six children in the garden.
- Plan what the garden can offer that week, such as harvesting, planting, watering or looking closely.

## Set up

- Walk the garden for hazards, such as tools left out, wet areas, poison oak and poison hemlock.
- Set out watering cans, child-sized tools, magnifiers and baskets.
- Set a handwashing station.

## Who does what

- Our garden educator leads the visit.
- The visiting educators stay with their own children the whole time.

## How the visit flows

- Welcome and our garden agreements.
- Exploring in small groups.
- A harvest, planting or watering, when the season offers one.
- Handwashing and goodbye.

## Safety

- One adult to six children in the garden.
- Shoes in the garden.
- Tasting only what our garden educator offers, after the allergy check. We are a nut free campus.
- Animals visited only with our garden educator.

## Cleanup

Return the tools, rinse the watering cans and compost any scraps.

## Afterward

Note what the children found and wondered about in the gathering's Afterward.

# Family Work Days

Families work beside us to care for our school, inside and out. Each task is a station from a job card with its point person, and its station cards print from the Work Day in Gatherings. Hours count toward family participation.

## What it holds to

- Families care for the place their children love, and children see them do it.
- Every task leaves the school safer, calmer and more ready for play.
- Children may help at the children's station, always with their own family.

## Before

- Choose the stations from the job cards, with a point person and spots for each.
- Gather the supplies for each station.
- Mark the work day ready so families can sign up on the Family page.

## Set up

- Put each station's card and supplies in its place.
- Set the children's station with small watering cans and a bin for special rocks.
- Set out water, snacks and a first aid kit.

## Who does what

- Each point person explains their station and checks the finished work.
- One educator moves between stations, answers questions and watches for safety.

## Stations we often need

- Wood chips on bare ground, under the gazebos and in the West Yard, thick under climbing structures and kept a little away from tree trunks and posts.
- Weeding the tree rings, the piazza and the West Yard. Weeds go where the educator on site directs, with nothing plastic in the animal pile.
- Planting along the front fence.
- Washing and sorting toys, removing anything broken or with small loose parts.
- Sifting and leveling the sandbox.
- Scrubbing the mud kitchen pots and setting them at child height.
- Scrubbing outdoor tables and indoor chairs.
- Organizing the outdoor shed, with heavy things low and sharp tools out of reach.
- Rearranging the indoor and outdoor piazzas for clear paths and easy supervision.
- A splinter and bolt check on fences, gazebos, benches and play structures.
- Making books for the classes.

## Safety

- Water breaks often.
- Bleach buckets stay high and away from children, and surfaces are rinsed well.
- Only adults use the power washer, with no children nearby.
- Children stay with their own family and away from power tools and cleaning supplies.
- Lift with your legs.

## Cleanup

Return tools and supplies, empty buckets, check every station and collect lost items.

## Afterward

Write what was done in the gathering's Afterward. Families log their own hours after the day on the Family page.

# Open House

Before the school year begins, families and children visit their classes, meet their educators and see the spaces. Families also sign up as class parent representatives and for the Parent Advisory Council.

## What it holds to

- A family walking out feeling that they and their child are known here.
- Children explore at their own pace.
- A short, warm exchange with every family matters more than long talks with a few.

## Before

- Each class prepares its Classroom Family Display for the entrance.
- Family index cards, one at each child's space.
- Sign-up sheets for class parent representatives and the Parent Advisory Council.
- Each educator's Beginning-of-Year Intention, ready to share.

## Set up

- The room calm, tidy and ready to be seen.
- The family display at the entrance and the sign-up sheets where families can find them.
- Educators in the room, easy to find.

## Who does what

- Each educator greets families by name where they can and introduces themselves first.
- Educators collect completed index cards as families finish them.

## What to share

- We see children as capable, curious and full of ideas, and the room shows it.
- The first weeks are about relationships, with children getting to know each other, us and the space.
- The curriculum grows from what children show us they are curious about.

## Questions families often ask

- What will my child learn this year? We observe first, then build curriculum from what children show us. Share what you are watching for now.
- How is rest time? Every child is offered rest after lunch, and no one is made to sleep.
- Can I volunteer? Point them to the class parent representative and Parent Advisory Council sign-ups, and the Family page.
- Who do I contact? Their class team, by email or 1Core.

## Closing

Begin winding down conversations a few minutes before the end. A family who arrives at the end is still welcomed warmly. If a sign-up sheet fills, start a second one.

## Afterward

Enter the class parent representatives and Parent Advisory Council members on the Family page, and note anything to follow up in the gathering's Afterward.

# Orientation

A family evening at the start of the school year. Families meet the people who care for their children, learn how our days and our thinking work, and begin to know one another.

## What it holds to

- Families leave feeling known and welcome.
- We share our image of the child, this year's lens, our principles and how we observe, plan and document.
- Families meet one another as well as us.

## Before

- Set the date with the director and add it to the calendar.
- Send the invitation, with a note that the evening counts toward participation hours.
- Prepare what families will see, such as documentation from our classes and the year's lens.
- Ask families about childcare needs and plan for children if they come.

## Set up

- Chairs in a circle where possible.
- Documentation displayed where families walk in.
- A welcome table with name tags and the sign-in list for participation hours.
- Water and a simple snack. We are a nut free campus.

## Who does what

- The director welcomes families and shares our principles and the year's lens.
- Each class team meets its families and shares how the day flows.
- One educator welcomes families at the door.

## How the evening flows

- Welcome and a chance for families to meet.
- Our image of the child and the year's lens.
- How our days, small groups and documentation work.
- Time with each class team.
- Questions and goodbye.

## What families take home

- Where to find what. 1Core, Kaymbu, the Family page and email.
- Family participation and how to log hours.
- How to reach their class team and the office.

## Cleanup

Put away chairs and displays, and collect the sign-in list for participation hours.

## Afterward

Note the questions families asked and anything to follow up in the gathering's Afterward.

# Class Evenings

An evening when a class team shares the ongoing projects of their groups with families. Families see the children's thinking through documentation, materials and the children's own work.

## What it holds to

- The children's work and thinking are the center of the evening.
- Educators share what they observed, what they wondered and where the work may go.
- Families are invited into the inquiry and their ideas are welcome.

## Before

- Choose the projects and threads to share.
- Prepare documentation panels, slides or the children's work.
- Send the invitation, with a note that the evening counts toward participation hours.

## Set up

- Display the documentation and the materials children used.
- Chairs for families, and a place to gather for the sharing.
- A sign-in list for participation hours.

## Who does what

- The class team shares the projects.
- One educator welcomes families and keeps time.

## How the evening flows

- Families walk through the documentation.
- The team shares the projects, from the moment each began to where it is now.
- Families share questions and ideas.
- An invitation to take part, such as bringing materials or sharing an expertise.

## Cleanup

Return materials and keep the documentation for the class.

## Afterward

Note families' ideas and offers in the gathering's Afterward and in the project in TREE.

# Welcome Play Date

A relaxed play morning at the start of summer school, so new and returning children and families can play in our yards together before the year gets busy.

## What it holds to

- Children play freely in a space that will soon be theirs.
- Families meet each other and their children's educators.
- It stays simple and welcoming.

## Before

- Set the date and send the invitation, with a note that it counts toward participation hours.
- Ask families to bring a snack to share, and remind them we are a nut free campus.

## Set up

- Walk the yards for hazards.
- Open the sandbox, water play, loose parts and the mud kitchen.
- A welcome spot with name tags and the sign-in list.
- Shade, water and a table for shared snacks.

## Who does what

- Educators welcome families, join the play and introduce families to one another.
- One educator watches the whole yard for safety.

## Safety

- Each family stays with its own child.
- Garden and animal areas open only with an educator present.
- Shoes in the garden and the animal yards.

## Cleanup

Children and families help put materials away, and an educator checks the yards and closes the gates.

## Afterward

Note new connections and anything to follow up in the gathering's Afterward.

# Community Welcome Gathering

A Saturday gathering in the first weeks of the school year for our whole community, new and returning families together, often around a shared meal.

## What it holds to

- New families feel part of our community from the start.
- Families from different classes meet.
- The Parent Advisory Council and class parent representatives are welcome to help host.

## Before

- Set the date and send the invitation, with a note that it counts toward participation hours.
- Plan the meal, such as a potluck, and remind families we are a nut free campus.
- Invite class parent representatives to welcome the new families in their class.

## Set up

- Tables and shade, with blankets for sitting.
- Open play areas for children.
- A welcome table with name tags and the sign-in list.
- Handwashing, water and compost and trash bins.

## Who does what

- The director welcomes everyone.
- Educators help families meet across classes.
- One educator watches the children's play areas for safety.

## Safety

- Each family stays with its own child.
- Garden and animal areas open only with an educator present.

## Cleanup

Families help clear tables and compost scraps, and an educator checks the yards and closes the gates.

## Afterward

Note what happened and any follow-up in the gathering's Afterward.

# Ice Cream Social

Our end of year gathering, when our community comes together on the big yard to share ice cream and enjoy each other.

## What it holds to

- A simple, joyful gathering to close the year together.
- Families of every class mix and play.

## Before

- Set the date and send the invitation, with a note that it counts toward participation hours.
- Ask each family to bring a topping to share, and remind them we are a nut free campus.
- Ask families to bring a blanket or chairs.
- Decide the plan for rain.

## Set up

- Ice cream, bowls, spoons and serving scoops.
- A topping table with labels, so families can see what is in each.
- Shade, blankets and handwashing.
- A welcome table with the sign-in list.

## Who does what

- Educators serve, welcome families and join the play.
- One educator watches the yard for safety.

## Safety

- Every topping labeled, with nothing that has nuts.
- Each family stays with its own child.

## Cleanup

Compost and recycle, wash serving tools and check the yard.

## Afterward

Note what happened in the gathering's Afterward.

# Graduation

North and South classes celebrate the children moving on to TK and Kindergarten, with all graduating and returning children and their families. The timeline is kept in Policies and Procedures, under School Events.

## What it holds to

- The children plan the celebration, from decorations and ideas to how it unfolds.
- Every educator shares a brief word.
- Many children stay with us for TK, and the celebration honors every child's next step.

## Before

- Give the class ample time to plan, and follow the children's vision.
- Choose a song that holds meaning for the year.
- Each educator chooses a brief talking point.
- Send the invitation to families.

## Set up

- Outdoors where possible, with seating for families and shade.
- The decorations the children made.
- When North and South celebrate one after another, leave time between to reset the space, or use two areas.

## Who does what

- The class team leads its own graduation.
- One educator welcomes families.

## How it flows

Follow the Suggested Graduation Timeline in Policies and Procedures, School Events.

## Cleanup

Children and families help take down decorations, and the space is reset.

## Afterward

Note the moments to remember in the gathering's Afterward.

# First Friday Morning Coffee, Tea and Chat

On the first Friday of each month, the director hosts coffee, tea and conversation out front after drop-off. Any family may stop by, and the Parent Advisory Council decides whether this is their gathering or they hold another.

## What it holds to

- An easy way for families to meet each other and the director.
- Short, warm and open to everyone.
- Better together for the children.

## Before

- Add it to the calendar each month.
- Remind families in the newsletter.

## Set up

- Coffee, tea, cups and a small table out front.
- A few chairs.

## Who does what

The director hosts. Parent Advisory Council members and class parent representatives are welcome to invite and welcome families.

## Cleanup

Bring in the table, cups and chairs.

## Afterward

Note ideas or concerns families raised that need follow-up.
